title: The dual LP and what its variables price

questions.heading: Any Nonnegative Prices on the Rows Give an Upper Bound
questions.stem: A maximization LP has two rows: hours (at most 40) and parts (at most 30). Activity A uses 1 hour and 1 part per unit and earns 5; activity B uses 2 hours per unit and earns 6. A colleague prices hours at 3 and parts at 1. What do these prices prove?

options.text: A bound of 150, because every price is nonnegative
options.says: Nonnegative prices are needed but not enough: they must also cover every activity, and A earns 5 while its hour and part cost 3 + 1 = 4.

options.text: A bound of 120, because only the hours row is priced high
options.says: A bound comes from covering prices only, and these leave A uncovered whichever rows you count.

options.text: No bound, because activity A is not covered by the prices
options.says: Right: A earns 5 per unit but its column costs only 3 + 1 = 4 at these prices, so a plan heavy in A could beat any number they give.

options.text: No bound, because a price must be positive on every row
options.says: A price of 0 is allowed: the lesson's own optimal prices put 0 on the transmission crews and still prove the optimum.

questions.heading: Each Dual Variable Prices One Unit of Its Row's Limit
questions.stem: A port's LP has optimal prices of 0.5 on its budget row, 0 on its crane-hours row and 1.2 on its permit row. The optimal plan leaves 40 crane hours unused. Operations offers 20 more crane hours, nothing else changing. What happens to the optimal value?

options.text: No change, because a row with room left is priced at zero
options.says: Right: a row with slack has price 0, and more of an unused resource leaves the best plan where it is.

options.text: A rise of 24, since the permit row's price applies to the new hours
options.says: Each price belongs to its own row: the permit's 1.2 prices permits, not crane hours.

options.text: A rise of 10, since each new hour is worth the budget row's price
options.says: Each row has its own price; the budget's 0.5 prices budget, and the crane row's price is 0.

options.text: A fall of 20, since idle hours count against the plan's value
options.says: Raising a <= row's limit can only allow more plans, so the value cannot fall; its price is nonnegative.

questions.heading: A Row's Direction Sets the Sign of Its Price
questions.stem: A maximization LP for a quarry has the row 'deliver at least 50 tonnes of gravel to the county', and the row binds at the optimum. What sign can its optimal price have?

options.text: Nonnegative, because raising any right-hand side gives the plan room
options.says: That holds for a <= limit. Raising a minimum removes plans, so a >= row's price is at most 0.

options.text: Either sign, because the row binds and a binding row's price is free
options.says: Only an equality row has a free price; the sign rule depends on the row's direction, not on whether it binds.

options.text: Only zero, because the minimum is met and costs the plan nothing
options.says: Price 0 is forced only on a row with slack. The vegetation floor binds and its price is -0.12.

options.text: Nonpositive, because raising the minimum can only remove plans
options.says: Right: in a maximization a >= row's price is at most 0, since a higher requirement can only lower the best value.
